planting.note: Direct-sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed; vines need ample room to trail.

directions: This AAS-winning pumpkin produces flattened, 9-10 pound fruit with pale blue-gray skin and deep orange, non-stringy flesh prized for baking and roasting. It matures earlier than many comparable blue pumpkins and shows good tolerance to powdery mildew. Vigorous trailing vines need a full season and plenty of garden space to size up fruit properly. Harvest when the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry and corky.

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil is warm; semi-vining habit still benefits from generous spacing.

directions: Jester stands out for its bumpy, salmon-red rind and deeply flattened, ribbed shape, offset by surprisingly bright yellow flesh inside. Fruit average 7-10 pounds and work equally well as fall decoration or as a cooking pumpkin. The semi-vining plants set fruit early and reliably for a specialty pumpkin. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot for a week to toughen the skin before storing.

planting.note: Direct-sow in warm soil; long vines need room to ramble.

directions: This hybrid butternut-type squash forms blocky, deeply ridged fruit that ripen from green to a distinctive tan rind dusted with a frosty white bloom. The deep orange flesh is dense and sweet with nutty, earthy undertones similar to standard butternut but richer. Vines are heavy producers, often setting 8-10 fruit averaging around 4 pounds each. Fruit store exceptionally well, holding good quality for up to four months after curing.

planting.note: Direct-sow after soil warms; vigorous vines need standard squash spacing.

directions: Mambo bridges buttercup and kabocha squash types, forming a classic blocky, squat shape with little to no 'button' on the blossom end. The rind holds an exceptionally dark green color even after months in storage, distinguishing it from older kabocha varieties that fade. Fruit average 3-4 pounds and yield uniformly across the vine, making this a reliable producer for market growers and home gardeners alike. Flesh is dense and sweet, best enjoyed after a few weeks of curing to build sugars.

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil is warm; allow full vine spacing for best yields.

directions: Winter Sweet is a kabocha squash notable for its unusual light gray rind mottled with charcoal, a departure from the typical deep green or orange kabocha skins. Fruit average 4-5 pounds and are prized for exceptional eating quality, with a flaky texture and deep, sweet flavor that continues to improve in storage. Peak eating quality develops two to five months after harvest, making it an excellent long-season keeper. Cure in a warm spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool, dry storage.
